reviewedChapters.decision: unchanged: accepted pilot handshake and identity maps already answer the chapter questions; resumption variants need qualification, not another overview

figures.question: What does each successful boundary still leave unproved?
figures.misconception: An address answer or an open port proves service identity and application health.
figures.alt: DNS candidates lead to TCP connection, verified TLS, HTTP interpretation and application outcome checks; each arrow requires new evidence.
figures.caption: Read downward as increasingly strong, separate evidence. DNS supplies candidates, TCP establishes a byte-stream connection, verified TLS establishes the intended service under configured checks, and HTTP/application checks establish their own outcomes. Success at one boundary does not certify the next. This HTTPS-over-TCP example omits routing/link details and optional proxy hops; it is a responsibility map, not a packet trace or a universal protocol stack.

figures.question: Why can old-endpoint traffic continue after an authoritative DNS update?
figures.misconception: A DNS TTL update expires every cache and moves an existing connection.
figures.alt: Client queries a recursive resolver, which queries the authority on a miss or expiry; an authority update leaves the eligible cached answer and an existing socket with independent lifetimes.
figures.caption: One ordinary positive A-record cache example from the lesson: the resolver caches old for 60 seconds at t=0, the authority changes at t=10, and t=30 can still return old. Refresh after expiry can select new while the t=5 connection remains independently usable. Time labels are illustrative seconds, not observations or synchronized update guarantees. Delegations, local/OS caches, aliases, negative caching and qualified stale answers are omitted; NXDOMAIN, NODATA and SERVFAIL remain distinct outcomes as explained below.

figures.question: Which constraint protects the receiver, and which responds to the network path?
figures.misconception: Local write pressure, the receive window and the congestion window measure the same resource.
figures.alt: Receiver window rwnd and congestion window cwnd jointly limit flight; outstanding bytes reduce new allowance, while Node write pressure is a separate local boundary.
figures.caption: Receiver-advertised rwnd protects receive capacity; sender-maintained cwnd limits flight according to congestion control. A simplified ordinary sender allows flight up to min(rwnd, cwnd), with already outstanding bytes reducing new allowance. Application supply and host limits can constrain it further. Node write(false) concerns a separate local buffering boundary, not a measurement of either window. No algorithm, tuning value, packet timing or drain-pressure experiment is implied. This adds a different mechanism beside the preserved TCP pilot figures.

figures.question: When may more bytes advance the parser, and when is this exchange terminal?
figures.misconception: Incomplete EOF can be repaired by pushing more data after end.
figures.alt: Open retains or emits frames on valid pushes; clean EOF enters Ended, residual EOF or a bound violation enters Failed; neither terminal state reopens.
figures.caption: This is the lab parser lifecycle, with header/payload waiting inside Open. A valid push can retain a partial frame or emit complete frames and remain Open. Clean EOF requires no residual bytes; incomplete EOF and any fixture bound violation fail terminally. Ended and Failed reject later input without reopening. The adjacent text supplies the two-byte/eight-byte format, per-push bounds and the partial-result caveat; the drawing does not promise partition-independent visibility on invalid input or production parser safety.

figures.question: When is a sequence gap provisional, and how does a duplicate change the count?
figures.misconception: A missing sequence at one instant proves permanent packet loss.
figures.alt: Receiver observes X:10, X:12, then X:11 and another X:12; the provisional gap fills and the final arrival is a duplicate within session X.
figures.caption: Illustrative arrivals for one known producer/session X, matching the later worked example. After X:12, X:11 is only not yet observed; its later arrival fills the gap. The second X:12 is a duplicate within this scope: four arrivals, three unique references. Arrows show application observations, not measured packet paths or UDP reliability. A different session needs its own sequence scope; cutoff, retention and authentication still require an application contract.

figures.question: How can complete HTTP responses still report unfinished or rejected work?
figures.misconception: Any 2xx response establishes successful completion of the business action.
figures.alt: Caller receives complete 202 acceptance, later retrieves a complete 200 whose representation says rejected; status and framing completion do not decide the business outcome.
figures.caption: A conceptual version of the import example below: the complete 202 reports acceptance and supplies a reference, then a later complete 200 representation reports a rejected domain result. A reference is an illustrative product contract, not a mandatory HTTP workflow. Informational responses, headers/body delivery detail, method safety and idempotence rules are covered in the retained text; neither 2xx status certifies durable product success.

figures.question: Why does the same EOF establish different HTTP completion results?
figures.misconception: A graceful TCP EOF proves a complete response body.
figures.alt: Length-delimited and chunked responses can be incomplete at EOF; a close-delimited response can be HTTP-complete while application content remains insufficient.
figures.caption: Three separate ordinary HTTP/1.1 response examples, after applying the body-length precedence rules below. Content-Length 3 plus only ab is incomplete; chunked content without its final chunk and trailer-section termination is incomplete. A response genuinely delimited by close can be HTTP-complete with ab at EOF, while still failing an application expectation of abc. The groups are alternatives, not three stages of one connection. HEAD, no-body statuses, CONNECT and ambiguous framing are intentionally outside these examples.

figures.question: Why can receiving headers leave a pool slot occupied?
figures.misconception: The response callback releases the connection and maxSockets bounds all queued work.
figures.alt: Admission and pool wait precede socket assignment and headers; the caller still owns bounded body consumption or cancellation before resources can be released.
figures.caption: A normal HTTP/1.1 client ownership path: queue wait belongs to total elapsed time, new sockets need setup, and reused sockets can skip it. Headers transfer body-cleanup responsibility rather than proving completion. Bounded successful consumption may permit reuse when framing and connection policy allow it; cancellation can sacrifice the connection. The map does not promise fairness, prompt queued-abort events or an API shared with fetch. The exact Agent fixture below remains the execution authority.

figures.question: When may a retained prefix safely be extended rather than replaced?
figures.misconception: Any successful response to a Range request may be appended.
figures.alt: A retained abc prefix and If-Range A can lead to validated 206 def, or a full 200 after change; the full response cannot be appended to the old prefix.
figures.caption: Two alternatives from the later abcdef example: the client retains abc with strong tag A and asks for bytes 3 onward using If-Range A. An applicable matching response can provide def as 206 with inclusive range 3–5/6; validate identity, coding, offset, length and completeness before appending. A changed representation yields full 200 in this example and must be handled as replacement/restart, never appended. Servers can ignore Range under the rules, and 416 is a separate outcome; this is not a general downloader algorithm.

figures.question: Which identity and protocol facts survive TLS termination as evidence?
figures.misconception: Front-side TLS and a forwarding header authenticate the backend caller end to end.
figures.alt: Client h2 TLS ends at ingress, which opens a separate HTTP/1.1 hop; backend sees ingress as peer and must evaluate original-caller assertions and upstream protection separately.
figures.caption: An illustrative terminating ingress: h2 over TLS at the front can become HTTP/1.1 on a separate upstream connection. Backend socket-peer evidence identifies the ingress, while original-caller fields remain assertions requiring established ingress trust and sanitization. Upstream encryption/identity must be checked on that hop; the drawing deliberately does not assume them. Pass-through, NAT and full forwarding-chain parsing differ and are omitted. This is a boundary illustration, not a prescribed deployment.

figures.question: Why can one HTTP/2 stream wait while another progresses, yet both share a limit?
figures.misconception: Multiplexed streams have independent transport and unlimited DATA credit.
figures.alt: With A credit zero, B credit 2048 and connection credit 512, A waits and B can send at most 512 DATA payload bytes; HEADERS and TCP have separate constraints.
figures.caption: A snapshot of server-to-client DATA allowance before any further credit arrives: A has 0 stream credit; B has 2048; the shared connection has 512. A waits, and B can use at most 512 flow-controlled payload bytes, consuming shared allowance. HEADERS are outside DATA flow control, but still face metadata and other resource limits. TCP ordering/loss and shared congestion can constrain every stream independently of these windows. This is protocol arithmetic, not a measured Node buffer state or a schedule.

figures.question: Which transport and protection boundaries change between HTTPS versions?
figures.misconception: HTTP/3 is HTTP/2 with UDP substituted underneath ordinary TLS records.
figures.alt: Separate groups map HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 to TLS over TCP, while HTTP/3 maps to QUIC streams with integrated TLS handshake and packet protection over UDP.
figures.caption: Three ordinary HTTPS mappings, grouped separately rather than connected as a migration sequence. HTTP/1.1 and h2 use TLS over ordered TCP; h3 uses QUIC over UDP. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3 handshake mechanisms and packet protection rather than putting ordinary TLS records on a TCP stream. HTTP semantics remain shared. Cleartext HTTP variants, tunnels and optional datagrams are omitted; the diagram claims no runtime support, deployment choice or performance advantage.

figures.question: Which missing byte blocks its own QUIC stream, and which dependencies remain shared?
figures.misconception: QUIC eliminates every cross-stream stall or uses packet numbers as stream offsets.
figures.alt: A waits for missing offset zero while B can deliver xy from its own contiguous offsets; shared connection resources and QPACK dependencies remain separate possible stalls.
figures.caption: The single-byte-offset model from this lesson, shown before A offset 0 arrives. A has offset 1 = b and cannot deliver a contiguous prefix; B has offsets 0 = x and 1 = y and can deliver xy. Independent stream ordering removes the shared TCP-sequence dependency, not connection credit, congestion, path or CPU constraints. QPACK can separately block header decoding. Boxes represent stream bytes, not QUIC packets; one packet can contain several streams and recovery uses newly numbered packets. No QUIC traffic or latency is measured.

figures.question: Can ping progress before a fragmented message ends, and what does close establish?
figures.misconception: A pong or clean close acknowledges durable processing of every business message.
figures.alt: After valid 101 opening, text fragments hel and lo surround a ping and pong; one hello message results, and a later close exchange does not certify business processing.
figures.caption: One HTTP/1.1 WebSocket opening and control path from the lab: a valid 101 opens the channel, hel plus lo form one text message, and ping/pong can progress between fragments. The displayed pong-before-continuation order is one permitted illustrative ordering, not a claimed measured packet order. The client-initiated Close/Close exchange ends this connection; a new opening does not restore subscriptions or missed business state. Masking details, errors, simultaneous close, TLS and extension variants are omitted; a pong and code 1000 supply no durable business acknowledgment.

figures.question: What survives incomplete EOF, and what must the server provide after reconnect?
figures.misconception: Reconnection and Last-Event-ID guarantee complete, exactly-once processing.
figures.alt: Blank-line termination dispatches event 7, incomplete EOF does not dispatch its tail, and a new request with Last-Event-ID 7 receives retained event 8 under this server contract.
figures.caption: A logical event/connection trace based on the local fixture: a blank line dispatches event 7, an interrupted tail at EOF dispatches nothing, and a new request can send Last-Event-ID 7. The shown server has retained event 8 and chooses to replay it. Reconnect transport behavior does not create history: expired/invalid cursors need an explicit gap policy, and repeated delivery remains possible. Arrows group text, not HTTP chunks. The lab reconnects manually with Node HTTP; browser EventSource scheduling, acknowledgment, durable retention and proxy flushing are untested.

figures.question: Which later evidence is still needed after HTTP 200 and two RPC messages?
figures.misconception: HTTP 200 or the first decoded message means a gRPC call succeeded.
figures.alt: HTTP 200 and two messages precede grpc-status 7 with end of stream; partial results remain observed while final protocol status reports call failure.
figures.caption: One conceptual gRPC server-streaming response over h2: initial HTTP 200 metadata, two length-prefixed messages that need not align with DATA frames, then nonzero final grpc-status and stream completion. The messages remain observed partial results while the call fails at its protocol boundary. Missing final status is not zero. A trailers-only response is another legal shape omitted here; this is a wire-contract illustration, not an executed gRPC integration, complete status-mapping algorithm or claim about durable business effects.

figures.question: Which mixed-version direction and rewrite path must compatibility evidence name?
figures.misconception: Both clients compiling or an additive field change proves all deployment directions compatible.
figures.alt: Old-to-new, new-to-old and intermediary rewrite paths are separate tests; each needs wire decoding, field preservation and semantic interpretation evidence.
figures.caption: Three distinct test paths, with no success asserted: old writer to new reader, new writer to old reader, and a read/rewrite path through an intermediary. Specify supported versions and verify decoding, retained fields and application interpretation in each. Wire acceptance can coexist with enum/default/presence meaning failures. The arrows express test direction, not guaranteed compatibility or deployment order; no schema or generated SDK is executed by this visual.

figures.question: What can the caller conclude when its deadline expires after the server acted?
figures.misconception: A client timeout cancels or rolls back an already performed remote action, making retry safe.
figures.alt: Service action precedes a response the caller does not observe in time; local deadline cleanup leaves the caller uncertain and does not erase the action or establish retry safety.
figures.caption: A permitted lost-reply ordering: the service receives a command, performs an action, and its response does not reach the caller before the caller stops waiting. The caller requests local cleanup but lacks a complete receipt, so its remote outcome remains unknown. The prior action is drawn as scenario knowledge, not client evidence or a durable-commit claim. A retry additionally needs replayable content, suitable idempotent/product semantics, remaining total budget and bounded policy; adding an idempotency header alone guarantees nothing. No cancellation propagation, rollback or timer measurement is implied.

figures.question: What extra step turns a plausible network story into a falsifiable investigation?
figures.misconception: A reset, status 200, or missing observation uniquely establishes root cause.
figures.alt: Observed boundary evidence leads to competing predictions and a scoped observation; inconclusive evidence loops back without converting uncertainty into a root-cause claim.
figures.caption: A diagnostic reasoning loop: preserve observer/attempt/phase evidence, state competing hypotheses with predictions, collect a scoped discriminating observation, and retain alternatives when it cannot decide. Explicit HTTP-completion evidence answers a different question from business outcome or root cause; missing/invalid completion remains unknown. Changed conditions narrow only the tested case. This diagram gathers no telemetry, invents no packet trace and establishes no production cause or learner competence.
